summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.executive_summary: This Feature Article reviews recent developments in bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic the dynamic functions of biological interfaces, specifically extracellular matrices (ECMs) and phospholipid bilayers. The authors highlight how self-assembling peptides and amphiphilic molecules can reconstruct these interfaces to facilitate regenerative medicine and drug delivery. A primary focus is on stiffness-controlled peptide hydrogels, such as A16G and A16G-Ncad, which mimic the structural and dynamic properties of scaffold cells to promote neuroblast migration in injured neonatal neocortex. The article details the design of JigSAP, a peptide with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces, which enables the efficient incorporation and sustained release of growth factors like VEGF, promoting angiogenesis in stroke models without cell transplantation. Additionally, the study explores redox-responsive peptides where the position of methionine residues controls the kinetics of gel-sol transitions, allowing for stimuli-responsive cargo release. The review also addresses the stabilization of phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) using metal-chelating peptides, which enhances their stability in blood circulation compared to spherical vesicles. Finally, it introduces an amphiphilic molecular machine (AzoMEx) that induces endocytosis-like membrane fission in liposomes, enabling the encapsulation and in vivo delivery of large biomacromolecules such as M13 phage viruses to multiple organs while retaining infectivity. These approaches demonstrate that bottom-up chemical methodologies can effectively manipulate bio-interfaces to create functional biomaterials for advanced biomedical applications.

Metal-chelating peptides stabilize phospholipid nanosheets for blood circulation.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This Feature Article reviews recent developments in bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic the dynamic functions of biological interfaces, specifically extracellular matrices (ECMs) and phospholipid bilayers. The authors highlight how self-assembling peptides and amphiphilic molecules can reconstruct these interfaces to facilitate regenerative medicine and drug delivery. A primary focus is on stiffness-controlled peptide hydrogels, such as A16G and A16G-Ncad, which mimic the structural and dynamic properties of scaffold cells to promote neuroblast migration in injured neonatal neocortex. The article details the design of JigSAP, a peptide with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces, which enables the efficient incorporation and sustained release of growth factors like VEGF, promoting angiogenesis in stroke models without cell transplantation. Additionally, the study explores redox-responsive peptides where the position of methionine residues controls the kinetics of gel-sol transitions, allowing for stimuli-responsive cargo release. The review also addresses the stabilization of phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) using metal-chelating peptides, which enhances their stability in blood circulation compared to spherical vesicles. Finally, it introduces an amphiphilic molecular machine (AzoMEx) that induces endocytosis-like membrane fission in liposomes, enabling the encapsulation and in vivo delivery of large biomacromolecules such as M13 phage viruses to multiple organs while retaining infectivity. These approaches demonstrate that bottom-up chemical methodologies can effectively manipulate bio-interfaces to create functional biomaterials for advanced biomedical applications.

Research Context
Various cellular functions occur through dynamic actions of biomacromolecules at bio-interfaces. Extracellular matrix (ECM) adheres to membrane protein receptors to regulate cellular functions. Phospholipid bilayers contribute to fundamental cellular activities like substance transportation. Stimuli-responsive transformation is a notable characteristic of phospholipid bilayers. Recent progress in supramolecular chemistry allows creating dynamic materials. Artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming materials are introduced.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop bioinspired supramolecular materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces. It is hypothesized that mimicking dynamic actions can develop biomaterials for regenerative medicine. The research focuses on constructing artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming materials. The goal is to apply these materials to injured brain regeneration. The study also targets in vivo cargo delivery for extended blood circulation. Self-assembling molecules like fibre-forming amphiphilic peptides are used for construction.

Methodological Details
Self-assembling peptide fibres are recognized as versatile supramolecular scaffolds. Peptide amphiphiles construct nanofibres by forming cylindrical micelles. RADA16 forms supramolecular nanofibres via β-sheet-type hydrogen bonding. A16G is a mutant of RADA16 with terminal alanine replaced by glycine. A16G forms curved fibres seen on transmission electron microscopy. Molecular dynamics simulations visualized similar self-assembling morphology. JigSAP consists of Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2 sequence with AXXXA motif. JigSAP forms nanofibres with an average width of 3.2 nm. JigSAP hydrogel exhibits a rigidity of 1.1 x 10^4 Pa. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets are formed by mixing dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine with Chol-MBP. Chol-MBP binds to two Cu2+ ions to inhibit dissociation. AzoMEx contains a diazocine core undergoing opening-closing motion. GUVDOPC/AzoMEx uses 180 µM DOPC and 20 µM AzoMEx.

Procedures And Architectures
A16G hydrogel containing A16G-Ncad facilitates neuroblast migration in vivo. Neonatal neocortex is injured at low temperature before hydrogel injection. JigSAP is dispersed in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium. Circular dichroism spectroscopy visualizes conformational change to β-sheet. EGFP-JigSAP is incorporated at 93 mol% efficiency. VEGF-JigSAP and JigSAP are injected into ischaemic stroke mouse models. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets are diluted to 0.2 wt% for stability testing. Cu2+ ions are added to maintain nanosheet structure upon dilution. Fluorescent Cy5-labeled vesicles and nanosheets are administered via tail vein. Blood circulation profiles are observed by confocal laser scanning microscopy. AzoMEx undergoes photoisomerization to change distance between cationic moieties. M13 phage virus is incorporated into deforming membrane area.

Key Results
Migration rate of neuroblasts was significantly higher on A16G-Ncad hydrogel. Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in A16G-Ncad hydrogel. EGFP-JigSAP incorporation efficiency was 93 mol% compared to 3 mol% untagged. 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP was released after 24-hour incubation. Released protein increased to 39 mol% after 168 hours. Double-positive cells increased when VEGF-JigSAP and JigSAP were used. Nanosheet structure was maintained after dilution with Cu2+ ions. FL DPPC vesicles were aggregated and clogged in blood vessels. FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in blood vessels. M13 phages were efficiently incorporated into GUVDOPC/AzoMEx. Spleen infectivity was [25.6 ± 13.2] × 10^9 virions/mg. Liver infectivity was [18.3 ± 3.2] × 10^9 virions/mg.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Fibrous self-assembly mimics structure and dynamic function of scaffold cells. This provides a novel strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy. JigSAP demonstrates wide applicability to controlled sustained release. Stabilization of bicelle morphology enables prolonged blood circulation. AzoMEx functionalizes GUV for endocytosis-like fission. This technology can be applied to in vivo phage display.

Contradictions And Limitations
The mammalian brain has a very limited capability of regeneration. Delivering sufficient neuroblasts to distant injury sites is a challenge. Incorporating and releasing secreted proteins are generally incompatible. Bicelles composed of surfactants are essentially unstable. A molecular approach for endocytosis-like transport remains unexplored. The materials science to reconstruct biomimetic interfaces is in its infancy.

Claims
Self-assembling peptides can mimic ECM dynamics to promote neuronal migration. A16G-Ncad hydrogel facilitates neuroblast migration. Dcx+ neuroblasts are abundant in A16G-Ncad hydrogel. Neuroblasts are sparse in A16G alone hydrogel. This offers a strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy.
JigSAP enables efficient incorporation and sustained release of growth factors. EGFP-JigSAP incorporation is 93 mol%. Release increases to 39 mol% after 168 hours. Untagged EGFP incorporation is only 3 mol%. Useful for artificial scaffolds for tissue regeneration.
Metal-chelating peptides stabilize phospholipid nanosheets for blood circulation. Nanosheets remain stable with Cu2+ ions. Nanosheets are homogeneously dispersed in blood. Vesicles are aggregated and clogged. Suitable carrier for whole body blood administration.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A16G shows lower stiffness than RADA16. JigSAP hydrogel shows strain thinning profile. Redox-responsive peptides show contrasting macroscopic properties. JigSAP-IMI-Ox remains dispersed in solution.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 shows neuroblast migration on A16G-Ncad hydrogel. Figure 4 shows JigSAP nanofibre formation and protein release. Figure 6 shows stability of DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets. Figure 7 shows M13 phage encapsulation and organ distribution.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is bioinspired supramolecular materials mimicking bio-interfaces. 2. The strongest evidence is efficient VEGF release and neuroblast migration. 3. The future path is developing regenerative medicines and drug delivery.
